q2 a and b are both grammatical and natural. In a, to is a preposition introducing organizing the weekend workshop; in b, to introduces an infinitive of purpose. Marking a wrong and teaching that to must take organize misinforms the learner.
findings.suggestedRepair: Replace a with an objective agreement error, for example Our club allocate resources to organize the weekend workshop, and explain that the singular subject Our club takes allocates in this sentence. Preserve b and c, then re-review the whole changed payload.

findings.evidence: Counting the shelves refers to counting shelf units, while the stock-list task normally requires counting stock. The target phrase and message structure remain correct.
findings.suggestedRepair: Use I have finished counting the items on the shelves, or I have finished checking the stock.

optionAudit.overallExplanationReviewed: The library is providing support to extend hours, so option a is correct.

options.text: to provide money, staff, or time for a particular purpose
options.explanation: Correct: It matches the library providing support to extend hours, Vietnamese: phân bổ nguồn lực.
options.evidence: Matches the allocation of money, staff or time for the stated purpose.

options.text: to save money by reducing evening services
options.explanation: Wrong: Reducing services is not the meaning of allocating resources; the source describes support for longer hours.
options.evidence: Saving money by reducing services is neither the phrase meaning nor the stated extension of opening hours.

options.text: to arrange books on the shelves in alphabetical order
options.explanation: Wrong: It describes organizing books, not providing money, staff, or time for evening hours.
options.evidence: Alphabetizing books is a different specific task, not the meaning of allocating resources.

optionAudit.overallExplanationReviewed: Option b uses to + base verb correctly; a uses an -ing form after infinitival to, while c uses a bare verb after for.

options.text: Our club will allocate resources to organizing the weekend workshop.
options.explanation: Wrong: The infinitive after to must be organize, not organizing, in this sentence.
options.evidence: Allocate resources to organizing the workshop is grammatical: to can be a preposition and organizing the workshop its gerund-participial complement, naming the activity receiving resources.

options.text: Our club will allocate resources to organize the weekend workshop.
options.explanation: Correct: It naturally means providing money, time, or people for the workshop purpose.
options.evidence: Allocate resources to organize the workshop is also natural: the infinitive states the purpose.

options.text: Our club will allocate resources for organize the weekend workshop.
options.explanation: Wrong: After the preposition for, use organizing rather than the bare verb organize.
options.evidence: For organize is ungrammatical in this clause; for organizing or to organize repairs it.

optionAudit.overallExplanationReviewed: The group must submit on time, so option c is correct.

options.text: to discuss the deadline without submitting anything
options.explanation: Wrong: Discussing without submitting does not finish anything by the required time.
options.evidence: Discussing a deadline without submitting does not mean meeting it.

options.text: to change the deadline to a later date
options.explanation: Wrong: Changing the date means postponing, not finishing by the required time.
options.evidence: Moving a deadline later is postponement, not meeting the required time.

options.text: to finish or submit something by the required time
options.explanation: Correct: It matches the group submitting findings on time, Vietnamese: hoàn thành đúng thời hạn.
options.evidence: Finishing or submitting by the required time is the contextual meaning.

optionAudit.overallExplanationReviewed: Option a uses met and the required determiner; b has the wrong past tense, and c omits the determiner.

options.text: Our team met the deadline and submitted the report before Friday.
options.explanation: Correct: It naturally means finishing and submitting on time with correct collocation.
options.evidence: Met is the past form of meet; the deadline supplies the singular determiner. Submitting before Friday is compatible with timely completion.

options.text: Our team meeted the deadline and submitted the report before Friday.
options.explanation: Wrong: The past tense of meet is met, not meeted.
options.evidence: Meeted is not the standard past tense; met is required.

options.text: Our team met deadline and submitted the report before Friday.
options.explanation: Wrong: The singular count noun deadline needs a determiner here; use met the deadline.
options.evidence: In this ordinary complete sentence singular count deadline requires a determiner: met the deadline.
